faq.answer: No. Actual danger, harassment, discrimination, self-defense training, competition rules, trauma-related safety, and power imbalance can produce similar behavior. Compare matched encounters and preserve safety before retaining a one-to-one subtype hypothesis.
faq.question: Do direct challenge, courage displays, and testing a perceived threat prove this subtype?

faq.answer: Use two tense encounters with danger, consent, exit access, power, and training matched, and record whether observable behavior changes when the matched condition changes.
faq.question: What makes the one-to-one Type Six comparison fair?

faq.answer: calm negotiation in safety, easy disengagement, and no repeated challenge after danger is matched are formal counterexamples that should reduce confidence rather than be dismissed as exceptions.
faq.question: Which restored-safety counterexample weakens the direct-challenge hypothesis?

sections.body_md: Within a Type Six core hypothesis, the one-to-one subtype may emphasize direct challenge, visible courage, and response to perceived threat. Check actual danger, consent, training, and exit access first, then keep the subtype idea secondary and revisable.
sections.title: State the tradition as a secondary testable idea

sections.body_md: Compare two tense encounters while matching danger, consent, exit access, power, and relevant training. Record whether the person seeks support, challenges directly, or leaves when those conditions remain stable.
sections.title: Use matched situations before interpreting the pattern

sections.body_md: The one-to-one label organizes direct-challenge observations; it is not evidence about bodily mechanisms, neural fight systems, attraction biology, or an inborn pairing response.
sections.title: Reject bodily and neurological mechanism claims

sections.body_md: A person may speak softly, leave, seek help, or use indirect resistance even when threat is salient. Those safer responses alone cannot prove or disprove a one-to-one subtype hypothesis.
sections.title: Allow behavior that looks unlike the stereotype

sections.body_md: Actual danger, harassment, discrimination, self-defense training, competition rules, trauma-related safety, and power imbalance can shape direct challenge. Address those safety conditions directly rather than translating them into personality essence.
sections.title: Audit material, institutional, and relational conditions

sections.body_md: Lower confidence when the record shows calm negotiation in safety, easy disengagement, and no repeated challenge after danger is matched, and preserve the environmental account as a live alternative.
sections.title: Use changed conditions as a disconfirmation test

sections.body_md: Instrument-specific evidence cannot establish universal subtype ontology or cross-cultural equivalence, and this page cannot forecast courage, aggression, compatibility, loyalty, or relationship outcomes.
sections.title: Keep subtype inference local and non-predictive

sections.body_md:
Duration: 5

Context: Select two similarly tense encounters and one safety-restored follow-up where direct challenge can be observed without creating new risk.

Observable signal: Record actual danger, consent, exit options, power difference, relevant training, the challenge used, and what happens when the person can safely disengage.

Page-specific signal: Compare directness only after danger, power, consent, and exit access are matched; note whether challenge softens when safety and choice return.

Alternative explanation: Test actual danger, self-defense training, discrimination, harassment, competition rules, trauma-related safety, and power imbalance.

Reflection prompt: Use the safest matched encounter to identify a non-subtype explanation for directness and reduce the hypothesis when that explanation fits better.

seo.description: Type Six one-to-one is a traditional subtype hypothesis about attention to direct challenge, courage displays, and testing a perceived threat. This pattern does not establish subtype because actual danger, self-defense training, discrimination, harassment, competition rules, trauma safety, and power imbalance may shape the same behavior. Matched danger, exit access, explicit consent, and interpersonal power guide this comparison.
seo.title: Type Six one-to-one: a direct challenge, courage displays, and testing a perceived threat hypothesis
